result:
The world at three in the morning is a different country. Refrigerators hum their one note. Streetlights draw halos in the damp air, and somewhere a fox pauses at the edge of a wet road, considering its own reflection. In hospitals, nurses walk the long corridors with the particular quiet of people who have learned that silence is a kind of medicine.

And the ocean, always the ocean. Right now, in the dark water off the continental shelf, lanternfish are rising — the largest migration on Earth, happening every night, unnoticed. Billions of creatures climb toward the surface to feed, then sink again before dawn, like a breath the planet takes and releases. We send probes to Mars. We still cannot say how many fish live in the sea.

I find this comforting. Not everything has been flattened into knowledge. There are still rooms in the world where the light doesn't reach, and things continue regardless — the octopus dreaming in its den, color moving across its skin like a mood made visible; the mycelial networks threading the forest floor, passing messages from tree to tree in chemistry older than language.

We talk about the world as if it were a finished thing, mapped and settled. But the night persists. The deep persists. Somewhere a lighthouse is still sweeping its slow arm across the water, keeping a promise nobody made, for ships that may never come. That seems like a decent way to spend a life, or a night: to shine without needing to know why.
